newsitem.title: MEXICO: Linguists attack Spanish as language of oppression.
newsitem.headline: Linguists attack Spanish as language of oppression.

text.p: More than five centuries after conquistadors invaded the Americas, the Spanish language remains an instrument of colonisation and oppression against millions of the region's Indians, according to linguists meeting in Mexico on Tuesday.

"The Spanish language has not been unifying a national community, as the education ministries have often believed in our countries," Carlos Montemayor, a member of the Mexican Academy of Language, said. "The spreading of Spanish has been one of the most aggressive forms of cultural destruction."

Montemayor spoke during the First International Congress of the Spanish Language, which began on Monday in the colonial city of Zacatecas in northern Mexico. Some 600 academics, writers, linguists and journalists are debating the problems of the Spanish language -- the world's fourth most widely spoken -- and its use in mass media.

Some 400 million people in 20 countries use Spanish as a first language -- mainly the result of Madrid's conquest of the Americas which began in 1492. Mexico is the world's most populous Hispanic nation, with 93 million inhabitants.
On Monday Hispanic Nobel Literature laureates Gabriel Garcia Marquez, Octavio Paz and Camilo Jose Cela sang the glories of Spanish, highlighting its flexibility and variety.
But experts on Tuesday warned that its spread threatened the survival of the 500 Indian languages still spoken by 40 million natives in Latin America. Some are almost extinct.

Montemayor blamed traditional Latin American education policy, which proposed spreading Spanish as a way to unify countries. "In some Indian areas families don't want their children to carry on learning the indigenous language, they want them to speak Spanish because they feel ... they will be better prepared to survive," he said.
"In Mexico some people are ashamed to speak indigenous languages," he added.

Mexican linguist Miguel Leon Portilla said the imposition of Spanish -- a process he termed internal colonisation -- could provoke violent reactions. Maya Indians in southern Mexico who launched a revolt in January 1994 had among their main demands more respect for Indian culture and language.

Leon Portilla suggested Latin American countries and Spain, which has Basque and Catalan-speaking minorities, recognise their multi-lingual societies in their constitutions and teach more than one national language in schools.
"The Spanish language has co-existed and still co-exists with indigenous tongues and, far from being endangered by this, is enriched," he said.

Some delegates said Latin American literature in Spanish had benefited from Indian cultural and linguistic influence, citing Guarani words in the writing of Paraguayan Augusto Roa Bastos, Quechua in Peruvian Jose Maria Arguedas's books and Quiche in Guatelaman Miguel Angel Asturias's work.

Mexican Spanish has been strongly influenced by Indian words. Mexican experts presented an "Index of Mexicanisms" including 69,566 variations registered since 1831, most derived from Nahuatl -- the language of the Aztecs -- or Maya.

Some Mexican Indian-inspired Spanish words have passed into other languages -- cocoa, tomato, avocado and chocolate, which all came from Nahuatl roots. Cigar and hurricane are words derived from Maya roots, some delegates claimed.
